meta.title: JARVIS — Homelab AI Cluster
meta.description: JARVIS — a private 18-node Kubernetes homelab in production: GitOps infrastructure, fully local AI inference, a fact-grounded voice assistant and a zero-trust network.

systemMap.title: The Entire Toolchain at a Glance
systemMap.description: JARVIS as the hub of six domains — from GitOps and local AI inference to security, voice and observability.

features.title: What JARVIS Does
features.description: From bare-metal node to speaking assistant — every capability runs on its own network, declaratively managed and versioned.

items.title: GitOps infrastructure
items.description: One Git monorepo as the single source of truth. Numbered, idempotent bootstrap scripts for the node layer, FluxCD for cluster state — every change a reviewable commit, every drift reconciled automatically.

items.title: 18-node bare-metal cluster
items.description: 14 Raspberry Pi 5, one Raspberry Pi 4, an ODROID-H5 and a GPU workstation joined as a K3s cluster with a highly available control plane — all self-hosted, no cloud VMs. Plus a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W as a watchdog outside Kubernetes.

items.title: Fully local AI inference
items.description: Requests run across tiered hardware — from Hailo NPUs on the Pis and a CPU reserve up to an RTX 5060 Ti workstation. No model call ever leaves the house.

items.title: Vision tracker (in preparation)
items.description: Planned: person detection with camera tracking via the conference camera. Processing fully local, storing only embeddings of enrolled people — never raw images.

items.title: Fact-grounded voice assistant & HUD
items.description: “Hey Jarvis”: on-device wake word, speech recognition and language model on the GPU, a British voice. Knowledge questions are answered only from cited sources (offline Wikipedia, news) with an automatic cross-check — in about one to two seconds. A holographic HUD shows search results, weather, media and system status.

items.title: Zero-trust network segmentation
items.description: Default-deny network policies per workload, WireGuard-encrypted node-to-node traffic in strict mode, a dedicated DNS filter and an explicit, versioned allow set instead of implicit reachability.

items.title: Security & compliance
items.description: Controls modelled on ISO 27001, NIS-2 and CIS: secrets only ever encrypted, signed and digest-pinned images, kernel-level runtime monitoring and automatic image scanning.

items.title: Automated version governance
items.description: Dependencies are checked continuously and proposed as reviewable pull requests — with a grace period for new releases, no silent “latest”.

items.title: Backup, DR & observability
items.description: Daily cluster backups and etcd snapshots to self-hosted S3 storage, tested restore paths, end-to-end monitoring and alerting across nodes, workloads, GPU and network.

items.title: Home automation & media
items.description: Home Assistant controls heating and devices by voice, knows the local weather and plays music and films from the NAS on the display, TV or speakers.

pipeline.description: Every layer of the cluster is managed by a dedicated tool; every change is a commit.

security.title: Aligned with ISO 27001, NIS-2, and CIS
security.description: Even as a private project, run like a production system — with documented controls instead of trust by word of mouth.
highlights: Encryption of sensitive cluster data at rest
Full API audit logging with RBAC traceability
Secrets stored encrypted only in the repository (never in plaintext)
Policy enforcement, runtime threat detection, and image scanning

In-kernel runtime enforcement (Tetragon): unauthorized process starts and connections by the AI services are killed instantly — on the Raspberry Pi nodes too, thanks to a purpose-built kernel compiled from signature-verified sources
Own container images are signed (cosign) and admitted only with a valid signature
Compromised upstream components are blocked and replaced — the AI gateway was swapped out entirely after a supply-chain incident
CI runs in hardened, isolated runners with no third-party actions; AI agents may only open pull requests, never run commands directly
Agents run isolated in a gVisor sandbox, with no service-account token and no host access
All Raspberry Pi cluster nodes are wired-only — Wi-Fi is disabled at the firmware level
Regular restore tests verify that the backups are actually restorable
security.footerNote: Infrastructure details, internal network addresses, and operational scripts stay private and are deliberately not published on this site.

items.title: The path of a voice request
items.body: The wake word “Hey Jarvis” is detected right on the voice terminal. The recording goes to Whisper on the GPU (under half a second); then Home Assistant decides: simple commands such as lights, heating, time or weather are handled instantly without a language model. Everything else goes to the local language model, which can use tools — web search, Wikipedia, weather, media, routes. Kokoro speaks the answer sentence by sentence: the first sentence plays while the rest is still being synthesised.

items.title: Grounded facts instead of hallucination
items.body: For knowledge and news questions Jarvis does not answer from memory. It looks things up first — in a complete offline copy of the German Wikipedia or through a self-hosted metasearch — and phrases the answer exclusively from those sources. Every number and date is checked against the source; if one lacks evidence, a second, stricter verification pass runs. If nothing is found, Jarvis says so honestly.

items.title: Home automation & n8n
items.body: Home Assistant brings together radiator thermostats, TV, speakers and weather data. Jarvis greets you on arrival with the weather and a rain preview and plays media from the NAS on the right device. n8n is ready for further automations; workflows are versioned in the same Git repository as the infrastructure.

items.title: The Kubernetes cluster (K3s)
items.body: K3s is a lean Kubernetes distribution for edge and ARM hardware. Three nodes form the highly available control plane with etcd, the rest work as workers. FluxCD continuously reconciles the cluster with the Git repository — manual changes are reverted automatically. Longhorn replicates storage across the nodes, Cilium encrypts all traffic between them with WireGuard. The complete state is reproducible from a single repository.

power.title: Estimated Power Consumption
power.description: An approximation based on the rated power draw of the hardware in use — not measured values, but a sense of the order of magnitude.
power.wolBody: The GPU workstation (HP Z840) has the largest single draw in the cluster at over 300 W peak. For fast voice answers it currently keeps the language model loaded permanently. Wake-on-LAN is prepared: in future it can sleep during quiet periods and be woken on demand, while a CPU reserve steps in briefly.
power.upsBody: An APC Back-UPS Pro 900 rides out brief outages and voltage dips so the nodes can shut down cleanly instead of losing power abruptly. Its own continuous draw — inverter standby plus trickle charging — is small, around 5 W.

askJarvis.title: Ask JARVIS
askJarvis.description: A prepared demo of how a conversation with the voice assistant plays out.
askJarvis.disclaimer: Pre-scripted demo: no microphone, no real AI, nothing leaves your browser. The voice — if available — comes from your device's local speech synthesis.

qa.a: All nodes are online. Flux reports no drift, the network policies are active and there are no open alerts.
Tomorrow will be cloudy with highs around twelve degrees, and rain is likely in the afternoon. I'd take an umbrella.

qa.q: How much power is the rack drawing?
qa.a: About two hundred and seventy watts right now. The GPU workstation keeps the voice model loaded so I can answer quickly.
